subject: Chemistry
title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids
summary: The carbonyl group (>C=O) is planar (sp²) and polar: the carbon is electrophilic, so aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition. Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones (less steric hindrance, fewer +I alkyl groups).
Aldehydes are easily oxidised, so they reduce Tollens', Fehling's and Benedict's reagents; ketones generally don't. These tests distinguish the two.
α-Hydrogens are acidic, which gives aldol condensation (with α-H) and the Cannizzaro reaction (without α-H). Methyl ketones give the iodoform test.

Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols and alcohols (resonance-stabilised carboxylate). Electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity. Their derivatives are acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters and amides.

formulas.name: Preparation from alcohols
formulas.formula: 1° alcohol + PCC (or CrO₃) → aldehyde;  2° alcohol + K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺ → ketone

formulas.name: Rosenmund reduction
formulas.mistake: BaSO₄ poisons the catalyst so the aldehyde is not reduced further.

formulas.name: Etard reaction and Gattermann–Koch
formulas.formula: toluene + CrO₂Cl₂ → benzaldehyde;  benzene + CO + HCl (AlCl₃/CuCl) → benzaldehyde

formulas.name: Nucleophilic addition
formulas.formula: HCN → cyanohydrin;  NaHSO₃ → bisulphite adduct;  ROH (dry HCl) → hemiacetal → acetal;  RMgX → alcohol
formulas.note: Reactivity: HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃ (sterics and +I effect).

formulas.name: Ammonia derivatives (addition–elimination)
formulas.formula: >C=O + H₂N–Z → >C=N–Z + H₂O  (Z = OH oxime, NH₂ hydrazone, NHC₆H₅ phenylhydrazone, NHCONH₂ semicarbazone)
formulas.note: 2,4-DNP gives an orange/yellow precipitate with all aldehydes and ketones.

formulas.name: Clemmensen and Wolff–Kishner
formulas.formula: Zn–Hg/conc. HCl  or  NH₂NH₂ then KOH/ethylene glycol:  >C=O → >CH₂
formulas.note: Clemmensen is acidic; Wolff–Kishner is basic — choose based on what else is in the molecule.

formulas.name: Cannizzaro reaction
formulas.note: One molecule is oxidised and one reduced (disproportionation).

formulas.name: Haloform (iodoform) reaction
formulas.when: Test for CH₃CO– and CH₃CH(OH)– groups.
formulas.note: Ethanol and acetaldehyde give it; methanol and propanal do not.

formulas.name: Acidity of carboxylic acids
formulas.formula: F₃CCOOH > Cl₃CCOOH > Cl₂CHCOOH > ClCH₂COOH > HCOOH > C₆H₅COOH > CH₃COOH
formulas.note: pKa falls (acid gets stronger) as −I groups increase or move closer to –COOH.

formulas.name: Decarboxylation and Kolbe electrolysis
formulas.formula: RCOONa + NaOH/CaO → RH;  electrolysis of RCOONa → R–R

examples.title: Tollens' test
examples.problem: How do you distinguish propanal from propanone?
examples.solution: Propanal (aldehyde) gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent and a red precipitate (Cu₂O) with Fehling's solution; propanone does not.

examples.title: Iodoform test
examples.problem: Which give the iodoform test: ethanol, methanol, propan-2-ol, pentan-3-one?
examples.solution: Ethanol and propan-2-ol (they oxidise to CH₃CO– compounds). Methanol and pentan-3-one have no CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)– group.

examples.title: Aldol or Cannizzaro?
examples.problem: Benzaldehyde with conc. NaOH; ethanal with dil. NaOH.
examples.solution: Benzaldehyde has no α-H → Cannizzaro: benzyl alcohol + sodium benzoate. Ethanal has α-H → aldol (3-hydroxybutanal), which dehydrates to but-2-enal on heating.

examples.title: Cross aldol
examples.solution: Claisen–Schmidt condensation: acetone (has α-H) forms the enolate, which attacks benzaldehyde → C₆H₅CH=CHCOCH₃ (benzalacetone).

examples.title: Acid strength
examples.solution: FCH₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > CH₃COOH > CH₃CH₂COOH. F has the strongest −I effect; the extra CH₂ (+I) weakens propanoic acid.

examples.title: Reduction choice
examples.solution: Clemmensen reduction (Zn–Hg/HCl) or Wolff–Kishner (NH₂NH₂, KOH, ethylene glycol): C₆H₅COCH₃ → C₆H₅CH₂CH₃.

topics.title: Structure and physical properties
topics.explain: The C=O bond is polar, so aldehydes and ketones have higher boiling points than hydrocarbons and ethers of similar mass, but lower than alcohols (no H-bonding between their own molecules). Lower members are water soluble. Carboxylic acids have even higher boiling points: they form hydrogen-bonded dimers.

topics.title: Oxidation tests
topics.explain: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO₃) → silver mirror; Fehling's solution (Cu²⁺ tartrate complex) → red Cu₂O; strong oxidants oxidise ketones only with C–C cleavage. Aromatic aldehydes do not give Fehling's test.

topics.title: Preparation of carboxylic acids
topics.explain: Oxidation of 1° alcohols and aldehydes, side-chain oxidation of alkylbenzenes (KMnO₄ → benzoic acid), hydrolysis of nitriles and amides, and Grignard reagent + CO₂ followed by hydrolysis.

topics.title: Reactions of carboxylic acids
topics.explain: With metals and alkalis (salts), NaHCO₃ (CO₂ effervescence — distinguishes acids from phenols), PCl₅ or SOCl₂ (acid chlorides), alcohols with acid (esterification), NH₃ then heat (amides), LiAlH₄ (1° alcohols). The –COOH group is meta-directing in electrophilic substitution of benzoic acid.

topics.title: Uses
topics.explain: Formalin (40% HCHO) preserves biological specimens; acetone is a common solvent; acetic acid (vinegar, ~6–8%); benzoic acid salts are food preservatives; esters give fruits their smell.

topics.title: Mechanism of nucleophilic addition
topics.explain: The nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon from above or below the plane, the carbon changes from sp² to sp³, and the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate picks up H⁺ to give the product.

ratta: Tollens' & Fehling's: aldehyde yes, ketone no.
Iodoform: CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)–; yellow CHI₃.
